title: RV Recall Updates | August 11, 2026
summary: Discover the latest RV recalls for August 11th 2026, including safety risks related to ladders and refrigerator ventilation.
body_text: Here’s a quick recap of this week’s NHTSA RV Recalls, along with some next steps for RV owners. Brinkley RV Recalls The exterior ladder on certain 2027 Model I travel trailers may have been installed outside of its designated support backer, allowing it to detach during use and cause a fall, potentially resulting in personal injury or death. Dealers will inspect and reinstall the ladder as necessary, free of charge. Owner notification letters were mailed on August 7, 2026. Learn more under recall #REC-2603 . Escape Trailer Industries Recalls Certain 2025-2026 Escape E13 travel trailers may have insufficient ventilation in the refrigerator cavity, allowing carbon monoxide to accumulate in or near the refrigerator compartment, increasing the risk of serious injury or death. Dealers will install a ventilation fan and insulation, free of charge. Owner notification letters were mailed on August 4, 2026. Learn more under recall #26V505 . Forest River Recalls The Federal Placard on certain 2027 Surveyor, Sabre, NOBO, IBEX, and UnMapped travel trailers may list an incorrect fresh water tank capacity, which could lead an owner to unintentionally overload the tank, increasing the risk of damage. Forest River will mail corrected Federal Placards to all affected owners and dealers for replacement, free of charge. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed by September 1, 2026. Learn more under recall #51-2076 . The printed circuit board (PCB) installed in the MaxxAir™ N-Series fan assembly on certain 2026-2027 Forest River Pause travel trailers and OG Luxury Coach motorhomes may have a defect that can cause overheating during certain operations, increasing the risk of a fire. Dealers will inspect the fan and, if the unit contains the suspect PCB, replace it with a corrected version, free of charge. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed by September 1, 2026. Learn more under recall #51-2077 . Certain 2027 Forest River Leprechaun and Freelander motorhomes may have been manufactured without a house battery circuit breaker, leaving a power wire without overcurrent protection and potentially leading to a fire. Dealers will install an overcurrent protection device, free of charge. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed by September 12, 2026. Learn more under recall #210-2085 . Grand Design RV Recalls On certain 2026 Grand Design Imagine travel trailers, a receptacle cover in the front pass through utility panel may have been fastened using incorrect screw holes, allowing a fastener to contact an energized 120V conductor and create a risk of fire. Dealers will inspect and correct the fastener placement, free of charge. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed between August 17 and August 21, 2026. Learn more under recall #910064 . The tire information label on certain 2026-2027 Grand Design Lineage motorhomes with the 20-inch wheel and tire package may state the incorrect rear tire pressure. Operating an over-inflated tire increases the risk of tire failure and loss of vehicle control. As such, these vehicles fail to comply with the requirements of Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) number 120, “Wheels and Rims – Other than Passenger Cars.” Dealers will replace the label, free of charge. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed between August 17 and August 21, 2026. Learn more under recall #M910065 . Certain 2027 Grand Design Imagine travel trailers may have been built with an undersized 30-amp circuit breaker on the inverter prep circuit. If an inverter is connected and the circuit is overloaded, the breaker may fail to trip, causing the wiring to overheat and creating a risk of fire. Dealers will replace the breaker, free of charge. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed starting on August 17, 2026. Learn more under recall #910066 . Jayco Recalls The certification label on certain 2026 Entegra Anthem motorhomes may list an incorrect tire size, which could result in the wrong tires being installed on the vehicle and increase the risk of a crash. Dealers will adhere a corrected certification label, free of charge. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed on August 24, 2026. Learn more under recall #9903662 . A brake pressure switch on certain 2024-2026 Entegra Anthem, Aspire, Cornerstone, Cornerstone Reserve, Reatta, and Reatta XL motorhomes built on certain Spartan K1, K2, and K4 chassis may retain residual air pressure, causing brake lamps to illuminate when the service brakes are not applied, which could confuse trailing drivers and increase the risk of a crash. Dealers will replace the pressure switch, free of charge. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed on August 31, 2026. Learn more under recall #26V484 . Newell Coach Recalls The steer axle air spring base on certain 2025-2027 Newell Coach P50 motorcoaches, may deform or crack during operation, causing a sudden loss of air pressure and suspension support, which could lead to an accident, serious injury, or death. Dealers will inspect and replace the air springs as necessary and add a support plate to the base, free of charge. Owner notification letters were mailed on August 3, 2026. Learn more under recall #26V488 . Winnebago Recalls The touchscreen display on certain 2024-2025 Winnebago Ekko motorhomes may register phantom touch inputs that transmit an unintended generator start command, potentially causing carbon monoxide to accumulate in enclosed spaces and increasing the risk of serious injury or death. Owners are advised to park outside until the repair is completed. Winnebago will deliver an over-the-air (OTA) firmware update correcting the touchscreen sensitivity threshold, free of charge. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed on August 24, 2026. Learn more under recall #208 . Are You Affected? Use your vehicle’s VIN to check if you’re affected by these recalls. title: First Citizens Bank Appoints Stacie Bales Barton and Sharon Thompson to Lead Growth Across Central U.S.

body_text: New Executive Vice Presidents will oversee Northeast Regional and Community West Regions RALEIGH, N.C. , Aug. 3, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- First Citizens Bank, a top 20 U.S. bank, today announced two additions to its regional leadership team. Stacie Bales Barton and Sharon Thompson have joined the bank as Regional Executive Vice Presidents, supporting First Citizens' continued growth and expansion into the Central U.S. Both will report directly to Ron Sanchez, Regional Executive Vice President at First Citizens Bank. Stacie Bales Barton Barton oversees First Citizens' newly formed Community West Region, which includes branches across Kansas, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Wyoming, Minnesota, Idaho and North and South Dakota. Based in Colorado, she brings more than 25 years of experience across several large financial institutions. Most recently, Barton served as Senior Vice President and Market President at BMO, where she led one of the bank's largest multi-state branch networks, spanning Northern Colorado and Wyoming. "Stacie's operational discipline and deep experience building high-performing teams make her the right leader to establish our Community West Region," said Ron Sanchez, Regional Executive Vice President at First Citizens Bank. "Her deep market knowledge and commitment to cross-functional collaboration will be instrumental as we significantly grow our presence in these markets and bring the full breadth of First Citizens' expertise to all of our clients." Sharon Thompson Thompson leads First Citizens' Northeast Regional territory, including St. Louis, Tennessee, Wisconsin and Northern Virginia. Bringing over 20 years of experience, Thompson most recently served as Chief Commercial Banking Officer at United Community Bank, where she led commercial banking strategy, risk, and growth. "Sharon brings a proven ability to align multiple business lines and geographies, which will be critical as we integrate new markets and continue to grow," said Sanchez. "Her track record of driving disciplined growth and building strong leadership teams will serve our clients and associates well across our Northeast Regional territory." The appointments support First Citizens' continued expansion following its agreement to acquire 138 branches across the central U.S., further cementing the bank's approach to community banking — pairing strong local relationships with centralized specialist expertise to expand access and bring high-touch service, banking products and deep sector expertise to clients and communities nationwide. "Together, their experience, leadership and proven results will play a key role in serving our clients' ambitions while advancing our strategic priorities and positioning our organization for long-term success as well," said Sanchez. About First Citizens Bank First Citizens Bank helps personal, business, commercial and wealth clients build financial strength that lasts. Headquartered in Raleigh, N.C., First Citizens has built a unique legacy of strength, stability and long-term thinking that has spanned generations. First Citizens offers an array of general banking services with branches and offices nationwide; commercial banking expertise delivering best-in-class lending, leasing and other financial services coast to coast; innovation banking serving businesses at every stage; and a nationwide direct bank. Parent company First Citizens BancShares, Inc. (NASDAQ: FCNCA) is a top 20 U.S. financial institution with more than $230 billion in assets and a member of the Fortune 500™. title: Fastest Way to Learn Spanish: 15 Ways to Speed Up Your Progress
summary: Holding a real conversation in Spanish, not just reciting textbook phrases but actually connecting with people, is a goal many learners share. The challenge is…
body_text: Holding a real conversation in Spanish, not just reciting textbook phrases but actually connecting with people, is a goal many learners share. The challenge is knowing which habits and methods move the needle fastest. Finding the best way to learn conversational Spanish comes down to prioritizing real speech patterns, consistent listening practice, and speaking out loud from the start. Parrot is an app built around exactly those habits. Rather than drilling grammar rules in isolation, it guides learners through the kind of practice that builds genuine fluency, making progress feel steady and measurable. For anyone serious about going from beginner to confident speaker, it offers a focused daily routine to learn Spanish . Table of Contents Why Everyone Wants the Fastest Way to Learn Spanish Why Most Attempts to Learn Spanish Fast Don't Work What Actually Makes Spanish Learning Faster 15 Ways to Learn Spanish Faster Is Learning Spanish Faster Actually Possible for Your Goal? How Parrot Helps You Learn Spanish Faster Start Learning Spanish Today Summary Knowing the 1,000 most common Spanish words covers roughly 88% of everyday conversation, according to frequency analysis of Spanish language usage. This means the vocabulary ceiling for functional communication is far lower than most learners assume. The barrier to conversational ability is rarely raw knowledge. It is consistent exposure to that vocabulary in context, across time, in formats that train listening and speaking rather than just reading. English speakers have a structural advantage that most learners underuse. Consistency outperforms intensity at every stage of language acquisition. title: EMR Automation Strategies (July 2026)
summary: EMR automation in July 2026: AI drafts notes, flags codes, and handles prior auth. See real time savings for therapy practices.
body_text: EMR automation has moved well beyond transcription. In 2026, systems draft clinical notes from ambient documentation, auto-populate billing codes, verify benefits before appointments, and route prior authorization requests without staff logging into multiple portals. The best EMR for physical therapy isn't always the biggest name. It's the therapy-specific system built for rehab workflows, where automation cuts the two-to-one EHR-to-patient-time ratio that drives clinician burnout. Whether you're comparing Empower EMR pricing, reading Empower EMR reviews, or Spry EMR against other options on a physical therapy EMR list, the core question is the same: does the automation actually reduce documentation hours, or does it add another system to manage? The real test is whether it handles FOTO measures, therapy cap tracking, and the functional outcome language your payers require, and whether it flags conflicts and maintains audit trails without breaking compliance rules. TLDR: AI drafts clinical notes from voice input and flags missing codes before claims go out in 2026 Ambient documentation cuts post-visit charting by roughly 45 minutes per day for many therapists Physicians spend two hours on EHR tasks for every one hour of direct patient care Therapy-specific EMR systems include outcome tracking (FOTO, OPTIMAL, PROMIS) tied to payer rules Prosper AI handles patient access and RCM workflows (calls, scheduling, benefits verification) at 60%+ end-to-end resolution in production, based on Prosper AI's customer deployment data What EMR automation means for healthcare in 2026 EMR automation refers to using AI and software to handle documentation, coding, and workflow tasks that previously required manual entry by clinicians or administrative staff. In 2026, this goes well beyond auto-populating fields: AI tools now draft clinical notes from voice input, flag missing codes before claims submission, and sync patient data across systems in real time. For physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy practices, where documentation volume is high and reimbursement often depends on precise functional outcome language, this matters considerably. Therapists using automated documentation tools report spending less time on notes and more time with patients. The shift is also reaching smaller settings. The best EMR for small physical therapy practices now often includes automation features once reserved for large health systems, making the gap between independent clinics and enterprise providers narrower than it has been. Core automation capabilities reshaping clinical workflows EMR automation in 2026 covers far more than just transcription. The most widely adopted capabilities across physical therapy EMR systems, occupational therapy EMR systems, and speech therapy EMR tools fall into a few key areas: Automation Capability What It Does Time Savings Ambient Clinical Documentation Captures patient-provider conversations and drafts structured notes in real time Roughly 45 minutes per day per therapist Automated Charge Capture Pulls procedure codes directly from completed documentation Reduces manual billing entry and claim errors AI-Assisted Prior Auth Checks eligibility and flags authorization requirements before appointments Less time on hold with payers Predictive Scheduling Analyzes cancellation patterns and waitlist data to fill open slots proactively Reduces unfilled appointment slots Ambient clinical documentation uses AI to capture patient-provider conversations and draft structured notes in real time, cutting post-visit charting time by roughly 45 minutes per day for many therapists. Automated charge capture pulls procedure codes directly from completed documentation, reducing manual billing entry and the claim errors that follow. AI-assisted prior auth checks eligibility and flags authorization requirements before appointments, so staff spend less time on hold with payers. Predictive scheduling tools analyze cancellation patterns and waitlist data to fill open slots proactively. These capabilities matter most when they write back into the EHR automatically. A workflow that requires staff to copy-paste AI output into a separate system trades one burden for another. How AI reduces documentation burden and clinician burnout Clinician burnout ranks among the most cited reasons for staff turnover in therapy practices, and documentation is a leading contributor. Research finds physicians spend roughly two hours on EHR tasks for every one hour of direct patient care. AI-assisted EMR tools are changing that ratio. Systems like Spry EMR and others built for physical, occupational, and speech therapy now use AI to generate draft SOAP notes from session data, auto-populate treatment codes, and flag missing documentation before claims go out. Recent studies on AI scribes show time savings vary by implementation, with some organizations reporting roughly 16 minutes saved per eight-hour shift. The practical result: therapists finish notes during or immediately after sessions instead of at the end of a long shift. For small and cash-based practices comparing the best EMR for physical therapy, this alone often decides the purchase. Fewer documentation hours also means fewer after-hours logins, which reduces the cognitive load that drives burnout over time. Accuracy and compliance in automated medical record systems Accuracy requirements in EMR automation are high. A misread medication dosage or a misfiled allergy record can cause serious patient harm, which is why healthcare organizations set strict validation rules before any automated entry reaches a patient chart. Most EMR systems now include built-in checks that flag anomalies before data is committed. These can catch duplicate entries, out-of-range lab values, and conflicting medication orders without manual review for every record. Compliance adds another layer. HIPAA governs how automated systems handle, store, and transmit patient data, and audit trails must capture every automated write action. Regulators expect the same accountability from an automated process as from a human one. Key areas where accuracy and compliance intersect in automated EMR workflows: Validation logic that cross-references new entries against existing patient records to catch conflicts before they're saved Immutable audit logs that record every automated action, including the source system and timestamp, for regulatory review Role-based access controls that restrict which automated processes can write to sensitive chart fields Exception routing that flags ambiguous or high-risk entries for clinician review instead of auto-approving them Specialty-specific EMR automation for physical therapy and rehab practices Physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy practices have documentation and compliance needs that general-purpose EMR systems often miss. Rehab-specific workflows (including progress note templates, functional outcome measures, and therapy cap tracking) require purpose-built tools. When choosing the best EMR for physical therapy or the best EMR for small physical therapy practices, clinics should weigh these factors: Specialty-specific templates that match physical therapy documentation software requirements, reducing per-visit charting time. Built-in outcome measure tracking (FOTO, OPTIMAL, PROMIS) tied directly to payer compliance rules. Scheduling and billing integration that reflects therapy-specific visit limits and authorization workflows. Occupational therapy EMR systems and speech therapy EMR tools that share a unified record, avoiding fragmented documentation across disciplines. Tools like Spry EMR and others on the physical therapy EMR list are built with these workflows in mind, as opposed to general EMR systems retrofitted for rehab use. Epic physical therapy documentation exists for larger health systems, but smaller cash-based practices often find it oversized for their needs, making the best EMR for cash-based physical therapy a distinct category worth reviewing separately. Implementation challenges and how to overcome them Healthcare providers adopting EMR automation often face a few recurring obstacles: staff resistance to new workflows, data migration complexity, and the cost of integration with existing systems. Staff buy-in tends to improve when teams see time savings early. Practices that run phased rollouts, starting with one department or workflow, often report faster adoption than those that switch everything at once. Data migration is where many implementations stall. Working with vendors that offer dedicated onboarding support and EHR-specific configuration reduces the risk of record errors during transition. Cost concerns are real, particularly for small practices. Many therapy EMR vendors now offer tiered pricing, and the return often shows up in reduced documentation time per visit instead of in headline feature counts. The providers who see results fastest tend to treat implementation as a workflow redesign project, not a software install. Cost, ROI, and resource considerations for automation projects EMR automation projects carry real costs that vary by scope, vendor, and integration depth. Most therapy practices can expect implementation fees ranging from a few hundred to several thousand dollars, plus ongoing subscription costs that scale with user count or patient volume. Cloud-based systems often reduce upfront infrastructure spend, but monthly fees accumulate over time. ROI tends to show up in two places: staff hours recovered from manual documentation and billing tasks, and reduced claim denials from cleaner, more consistent records. Practices that document fewer errors typically see faster reimbursement cycles . Smaller practices should weigh whether a full-featured EMR fits their actual workflow volume. Many cash-based or small physical therapy practices find that a right-sized system with focused automation features outperforms a bloated one with capabilities they will never use. Prosper AI's approach to automating patient access and RCM workflows Prosper AI sits in a different category from the EMR automation tools covered above. Where EMR systems manage clinical documentation, Prosper AI focuses on the patient access and revenue cycle management (RCM) layer: the phone calls, scheduling requests, insurance verifications, and administrative touchpoints that happen before and after a clinical visit. In physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy practices, front desks field hundreds of calls weekly . Prosper AI's AI handles inbound call volume so staff can focus on exceptions requiring human judgment. Key workflows Prosper AI covers: Inbound call handling for scheduling, cancellations, and rescheduling across high-volume therapy practices Benefits verification and prior authorization support , reducing manual back-and-forth with payers Patient billing, including handling billing questions and collecting payment Post-visit follow-up and RCM touchpoints that many narrow-scope scheduling tools leave to staff Prosper AI operates at roughly 60%+ end-to-end resolution in production (based on Prosper AI's customer deployment data), meaning the majority of routine calls get resolved without staff involvement. That kind of coverage matters for small cash-based practices and multi-site therapy groups alike, where front desk capacity is rarely a surplus resource. Final thoughts on automation in physical therapy and rehab workflows EMR automation earns its cost when it saves time your team actually gets to keep, not when it trades one manual process for another. Therapy practices see results fastest when they pick tools built for rehab workflows from the start, not general systems retrofitted later. Start with patient access and RCM if your front desk is the real bottleneck. Your documentation might be cleaner, but if staff still spend half their day on hold with payers or rescheduling no-shows, you're solving the wrong problem first. FAQ What's the best EMR for small physical therapy practice workflows that include automated documentation? Small practices typically see the strongest ROI from therapy-specific EMR systems that include ambient documentation, automated charge capture, and built-in outcome measure tracking compared to general-purpose systems retrofitted for rehab. Systems designed for physical therapy workflows reduce per-visit charting time by an average of 45 minutes per day and include templates that match payer compliance requirements for functional outcome language. EMR automation vs manual documentation: what are the actual time savings? Therapists using AI-assisted documentation tools report cutting post-visit charting time by roughly 45 minutes per day, with most finishing notes during or immediately after sessions instead of at end of shift. The ROI shows up in two places: staff hours recovered from manual documentation tasks, and reduced claim denials from cleaner records that speed reimbursement cycles. Can EMR automation handle prior authorization workflows without staff intervention? Most therapy EMR systems now include AI-assisted prior auth tools that check eligibility and flag authorization requirements before appointments, but the level of automation varies considerably by vendor. The most capable systems pull procedure codes directly from completed documentation and sync authorization status across systems in real time, reducing manual back-and-forth with payers but stopping short of fully autonomous prior auth completion in most cases. Best EMR for cash-based physical therapy vs insurance-heavy practices? Cash-based practices often find that right-sized systems with focused automation features outperform bloated enterprise EMR platforms built for large health systems. The key difference: cash practices need automated documentation and scheduling far more than they need complex benefits verification or therapy cap tracking, making specialty-specific tools like those on the physical therapy EMR list a better fit than Epic physical therapy documentation and similar enterprise systems. How does Prosper AI fit into EMR automation workflows for therapy practices? Prosper AI handles the patient access and revenue cycle management layer (inbound scheduling calls, benefits verification, and post-visit follow-up) that happens before and after the clinical visit, while EMR systems manage in-session clinical documentation. For high-volume therapy practices fielding hundreds of weekly calls, Prosper AI resolves 60%+ of routine scheduling and insurance verification requests end-to-end without staff involvement (based on Prosper AI's customer deployment data), freeing front desk capacity for exceptions that require human judgment.

title: Cloud GTM Glossary: 40 Marketplace Terms Defined
summary: A Cloud GTM glossary for marketplace sellers: 40 terms grouped by deal stage, from listing types and private offers to committed spend and payouts.
body_text: Cloud GTM is the go-to-market motion where software is sold, transacted, and billed through cloud marketplaces and cloud provider co-sell programs rather than only through direct contracts. This glossary defines the forty terms that motion runs on, grouped by the stage of a deal where you first meet them. Cloud GTM has a vocabulary problem. Three clouds invented the same concepts independently, gave them different names, and abbreviated all of them. The result is a field where a new alliances hire spends their first month decoding acronyms rather than building anything. This is the decoder. Terms are grouped by deal stage — landscape, listing, offers, committed spend, co-sell, channel, money — because that is the order you actually meet them in. The landscape Cloud GTM is the go-to-market motion where software is sold and billed through cloud marketplaces and cloud provider co-sell programs. It sits alongside direct sales rather than replacing it, and it changes who the customer contracts with, not who they buy from. A cloud marketplace is a cloud provider’s storefront where customers find, buy, and deploy third-party software, billed through the cloud account they already hold. AWS Marketplace, Microsoft Marketplace, Google Cloud Marketplace, Snowflake Marketplace, Alibaba Cloud Marketplace, and Oracle Cloud Marketplace are the ones ISVs sell on today. An ISV — independent software vendor — is a company that builds and sells its own software. On a marketplace, the ISV is the seller. A hyperscaler is one of the largest cloud providers: AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud. The term matters because co-sell programs exist at all three, while marketplace listings extend further. A cloud marketplace platform is third-party software that operates marketplace listings, offers, metering, and co-sell from one system instead of one console per cloud. How to choose a cloud marketplace platform covers the evaluation criteria. Buy with AWS lets a buyer start an AWS Marketplace purchase from the seller’s own website rather than from the marketplace listing, keeping the transaction on marketplace rails while the discovery happens on your site. Getting listed A listing is the product page plus the commercial configuration that makes your software buyable on a marketplace. It is not just a description — the pricing, dimensions, and legal terms live there too. A listing type is the delivery and pricing shape of a product: SaaS, AMI or virtual machine image, container, professional services, or data. Fees, contract mechanics, and buyer experience all differ by type. BYOL — bring your own licence — is a listing where the customer deploys software they licensed from you directly. The marketplace provides distribution, not the transaction. A free trial is time-limited or usage-limited free access granted through the listing, after which the buyer converts to a paid subscription. Free trials on cloud marketplaces covers how each cloud implements them. A technical review is the cloud’s assessment of your product before it can be listed or achieve certain designations — AWS’s Foundational Technical Review (FTR), Microsoft’s Partner Center certification, and Google Cloud’s architectural review are the three you’ll encounter. A seller console is the cloud’s own interface for managing listings and offers: the AWS Marketplace Management Portal, Microsoft Partner Center, and Google Cloud’s Producer Portal. Every cloud has one, and none of them talks to the others. Offers and agreements A public offer is the pricing and terms visible on your listing to every buyer. Also called list price. A private offer is a custom, non-public deal extended to one specific buyer, with negotiated pricing, a chosen term, and often custom legal terms. It is the construct most enterprise marketplace revenue closes on. An express private offer is AWS’s automated version: the buyer requests an offer from the listing and AWS generates it from rate cards the seller configured in advance. Express private offers, explained covers the setup. A private plan is Microsoft’s construct for a hidden pricing plan inside a public listing, visible only to tenants you nominate. Unlike a private offer, it inherits the public listing’s legal terms. An agreement is the contract record created when a buyer accepts an offer. It is the object your renewals, amendments, and cancellations act on. An entitlement is the record of what a buyer is entitled to use after purchase — the seats, units, or capacity your product should provision and meter against. A EULA — end user licence agreement — is the licence terms the customer accepts. A private offer can carry a custom EULA for that transaction; a public listing carries one for everybody. A standard contract is the cloud’s pre-negotiated legal template, offered so buyers and sellers can skip a redline cycle. Accepting one trades legal control for procurement speed. Committed spend Committed spend is money a customer has contractually promised to spend with a cloud provider over a term. It is the single strongest reason enterprise buyers prefer marketplace transactions. EDP — the AWS Enterprise Discount Program — is AWS’s committed spend agreement, where a customer commits to a spend level in exchange for discounts. AWS EDP: what sellers need to know covers the seller’s angle. MACC — the Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment — is Microsoft’s equivalent. What is a MACC? explains how marketplace purchases apply to it. Universal Cloud Credits are Oracle’s committed spend construct, drawn down by Oracle Cloud Marketplace purchases. Drawdown is the act of applying a marketplace purchase against a customer’s committed spend. It is why “buy it through the marketplace” turns a budget request into an allocation decision. Co-sell Co-sell is selling jointly with a cloud provider’s own field team, where the cloud’s sellers are compensated for driving your product into their accounts. ACE — APN Customer Engagements — is AWS’s co-sell system, where opportunities are shared between partner and AWS. AWS ACE: a practical co-sell guide covers how sharing actually works. An opportunity share , or referral, is the record you send a cloud provider describing a live deal, so their field team can engage. The quality of that record decides whether anyone does. Partner-sourced revenue is revenue on deals a partner or cloud originated. Partner-influenced revenue is revenue on deals a partner materially helped close but did not originate. Confusing the two is the most common cause of channel attribution arguments. MDF — market development funds — is cloud provider money for joint demand generation: campaigns, events, and content. AWS partner funding programs covers MDF alongside the other incentives. Channel A channel partner is a third party that sells your product to end customers — a reseller, a systems integrator, or a managed service provider. CPPO — Channel Partner Private Offer — is AWS’s construct for a partner-transacted marketplace deal, built from a base offer the ISV creates. A multiparty private offer (MPO) is Microsoft’s equivalent, where a channel partner sells and Microsoft invoices the customer. A reseller private offer plan is Google Cloud’s version: the ISV publishes a plan the reseller accepts once, and the reseller creates customer offers from it. CPPO vs MPO compares all three. Deal registration is the process where a partner formally claims an opportunity with you, protecting it from conflict and locking in their commission. Deal registration software for ISVs covers the lifecycle and where it breaks. Money A listing fee is the percentage a marketplace takes from a transaction. On AWS it varies by product type, offer type, and total contract value — what a marketplace dollar actually costs you works through the arithmetic. A disbursement is the payment the marketplace sends you after collecting from the buyer, net of fees. It arrives on the marketplace’s schedule, not your invoice’s, which is a working-capital question as much as an accounting one. Metering is reporting usage to the marketplace so it can bill a usage-based product. A metering dimension is the unit that usage is measured in — API calls, seats, gigabytes — and choosing it badly is expensive to undo. The seller of record is the party legally selling to the buyer. On a marketplace transaction, that is generally the cloud provider, which is what changes your tax treatment, your revenue recognition, and who the customer’s contract is with. Frequently asked questions What does Cloud GTM mean? Cloud GTM is the go-to-market motion where software is sold and billed through cloud marketplaces and cloud provider co-sell programs. It changes who the customer contracts with and how the purchase is funded. What’s the difference between a public offer and a private offer? A public offer is the list price visible to everyone on your listing. A private offer is a custom, non-public deal for one buyer, with negotiated pricing, term, and often custom legal terms. What does drawdown mean on a cloud marketplace? Drawdown is applying a marketplace purchase against money the customer already committed to spend with the cloud provider — an AWS EDP, a Microsoft MACC, or Oracle Universal Cloud Credits. What is the difference between an agreement and an entitlement? An agreement is the contract record created when a buyer accepts an offer. An entitlement is the record of what they can actually use — the seats, units, or capacity your product provisions against. What is a metering dimension? The unit a usage-based marketplace product bills on: API calls, seats, gigabytes, or similar. It is defined at listing time and expensive to change afterwards, so it deserves a real design decision. Who is the seller of record on a marketplace deal? Generally the cloud provider, not the ISV. That changes tax treatment, revenue recognition, and whose paper the customer signs — which is why finance needs to be in the room early. Takeaways The same concept has a different name on each cloud. Learn the concept — custom deal, committed spend, partner-transacted offer — and the acronyms sort themselves out. Committed spend is the centre of gravity. EDP, MACC, and Universal Cloud Credits explain most enterprise marketplace behaviour. Agreement, entitlement, and offer are three different objects. Teams that treat them as one cannot reconcile revenue. Partner-sourced and partner-influenced are not synonyms, and the difference is worth defining before your first commission dispute. Seller of record is a finance question disguised as a legal one. Raise it before the first marketplace deal, not after. New to the motion? The complete guide to Cloud GTM for ISVs puts these terms into the sequence a real marketplace program runs in.

How to Set Up VRBO Automated Messages for Every Guest
summary: VRBO automated messages have real limits. Property managers who add workflow automation close the gaps and scale guest communication without adding staff.
body_text: VRBO's built-in automation does less than most hosts think. Here is exactly where it stops, where it silently fails, and what that costs you at scale. Most vacation rental property managers and operations leads think that once they set up VRBO's built-in automated messages, their guest communication is on autopilot and they can scale without adding staff time to messaging. In reality, VRBO's built-in automation covers a narrow, fixed slice of the guest journey, and the gaps become costly well before a portfolio reaches meaningful scale. For operators building toward genuine scale, understanding exactly where the platform's automation starts and stops is the prerequisite for building anything better, including the kind of workflow-driven guest communication that runs independently of any single OTA. VRBO's Inbox is the central hub for all guest and host communication on the platform. From here, hosts can read and reply to messages, access saved templates, and review booking details tied to each conversation thread. What the Inbox does not do is act on any of this automatically. There is no logic layer that reads a booking, evaluates context, and sends a message without a host or team member initiating it. The Inbox is a well-organized dashboard, not an autonomous communication engine. VRBO does send one genuinely scheduled message on your behalf: an automatic welcome guide delivered to guests 7 days before check-in. That is useful, but it is also the ceiling. There is no equivalent scheduled message at booking confirmation, mid-stay, or post-checkout. One automated send across the entire guest journey is a starting point, not a system. VRBO's message templates let hosts save pre-written messages and insert them into conversations with a few clicks. There is no trigger logic attached to them. At three properties that is manageable; at fifteen, the manual overhead compounds into a material time cost every single week. 5x more likely to convert those inquiries into bookings compared to hosts who wait 24 hours or longer. A template sent manually after catching an SMS alert is still a manual process with a human failure point. That gap does not close by writing better templates. It closes by removing the human-in-the-middle entirely. Every manual touchpoint is a point where speed, consistency, and guest experience depend entirely on a person being available at the right moment, a dependency that compounds with every property added to a portfolio. Every manual touchpoint is a point where speed, consistency, and guest experience depend entirely on a person being available at the right moment, a dependency that compounds with every property added to a portfolio. 2.5x More bookings from fast inquiry replies Key takeaways VRBO's native automated messages cover booking confirmation, check-in, and checkout, roughly 40% of the guest journey, with no time-based triggers, no cross-channel logic, and no access to dynamic guest data. A saved VRBO template is not a live automation, two additional steps must be completed before any message actually sends, and most hosts skip at least one of them. Six message types form a complete guest communication workflow; VRBO's trigger architecture makes it structurally impossible to deliver all six without manual intervention filling the gaps. The inbox doesn't empty as a portfolio scales, it grows, because VRBO templates are static by design and can't adapt to booking context, guest behavior, or multi-property logic. Erwan Le Roy's 35-property operation reached a 96% automation rate not by perfecting VRBO templates, but by routing guest communication through a workflow layer that runs independently of any single platform. conduit.ai's Workflows close that gap by triggering automated sequences based on conversation events and guest data, so follow-ups, check-in instructions, and post-stay messages run as repeatable processes without manual effort, regardless of which OTA the booking came from. How to Access and Create Templates in VRBO - Step by Step Saving a VRBO message template feels like finishing the job. The interface accepts your text, your trigger, your timing, and then goes quiet, which most hosts reasonably interpret as confirmation that the automation is running. In practice, two separate steps sit between "saved" and "actually sending," and skipping either one means your templates exist on the platform while your guests receive nothing. One of the sharpest pain points hosts run into early is discovering that what VRBO reps describe as "automated messages" is not automation in the way most people mean it. What the platform actually provides are manual-use templates. You must still log in, select the template, and send it yourself. That distinction matters enormously when you are trying to keep guests, cleaners, contractors, and owners coordinated without sitting inside every thread. Conduit's AI Agents layer sits above platform templates precisely to close that gap: once your SOPs and manuals are connected, the agent fires replies continuously, before, during, and after a stay, without manual intervention on each send. Where to Find the Template Builder Inside VRBO's Inbox To access VRBO's Templates feature, open your Inbox , then select "Templates" from the left-hand navigation. From there, choose "Create new template." The full path is: Inbox Templates Create new template Write and name your message Set your scheduling trigger Save Activate That final activation step is where most setups stall, and no confirmation banner warns you that you missed it. Many hosts never find this path cleanly on the first attempt. Without clear, step-by-step guidance, the default workaround becomes copy-pasting messages outside the platform entirely, a manual habit that compounds as your property count grows. If you are managing communications across multiple properties or platforms simultaneously, that manual drag is where coordination breaks down fastest. How to Name and Personalize Your Template Using VRBO's Dynamic Tags Give each template a name that signals its trigger at a glance, "Booking Confirmed," "Day Before Check-In", so you can audit your sequence quickly. Inside the message body, the Personalize feature inserts dynamic tags that pull guest names, property details, and booking information automatically. Test each tag in a dummy booking before relying on it at scale; a tag that renders incorrectly in a real guest message is worse than no personalization at all. Hosts managing high volumes of repetitive guest touchpoints, check-in instructions, house rules, checkout reminders, benefit most from pairing VRBO's tag system with a structured message library. Conduit's Integrations can pull that existing content directly into your agent's knowledge base without manual re-entry, so your templates and your AI-assisted replies stay consistent with the same source of truth. The 'Always Send for Last-Minute Bookings and Short Stays' Toggle This is the single most commonly missed setting in VRBO's template builder. When a booking arrives close to check-in, your scheduled trigger may fall inside the lead time window and simply not fire. VRBO includes a toggle labeled "Always send for last-minute bookings and short stays" specifically to handle this scenario. For many urban and drive-to markets where a substantial share of bookings arrive close to check-in, this toggle is not an edge-case setting, it is a default requirement. Hosts who discover it after the fact usually do so because a guest arrived without check-in instructions. This is also the scenario where the gap between a manual template system and true automation becomes most costly. Response time directly affects your ranking on VRBO and Airbnb. A last-minute booking that slips through without a timely reply, because the toggle was off and no one was watching, is both a guest experience failure and a search visibility hit. Activating the Template, The Step Most Guides Skip Saving a template and activating a template are two different actions in VRBO's system. A saved template sits in your library. An activated template fires on schedule. After completing your message and setting your trigger, you must explicitly enable the template before it enters the automation queue. VRBO also requires a separate step to enable inbound message notifications in your account settings; without it, guest replies arrive silently. When using Conduit's Inbox to monitor conversations across properties, silent inbound replies are a known operational risk. The Inbox is designed for ongoing use by an operations or support team to review and manage all conversations the AI agent is handling, which means a missed VRBO notification setting can create a blind spot even when everything else in your stack is working correctly. Confirm notifications are live at the platform level before assuming your monitoring layer will catch everything. Troubleshooting, Why Your Automated Message Didn't Fire The most common causes of a silent template failure are: Activation was skipped The last-minute toggle is off The trigger window is set tighter than the booking lead time allows Start your audit by confirming each template's status shows as active, not just saved. Then verify the last-minute toggle is enabled for any message that needs to reach guests who book close to arrival, and confirm that message notifications are turned on so incoming guest replies surface in real time rather than arriving silently in the background. Conduit's Workflows layer adds the most value when your business has recurring, predictable guest touchpoints that currently require manual staff action, and it operates independently of whether the underlying platform's toggle was set correctly. Response speed at every touchpoint compounds into ranking outcomes, so closing the gaps in your trigger chain is not a cosmetic fix, it is a direct input to your listing's visibility. What Types of Automated Messages Every VRBO Host Should Send Six types of automated messages form the backbone of a complete vacation rental guest communication workflow. Hosts who treat each one as a distinct job to be done, not just a scheduled template, consistently see stronger review scores and fewer last-minute guest issues. Yet the sequencing logic matters as much as the messages themselves: VRBO's native triggers create a structurally incomplete guest journey map, firing only on booking-event schedules and leaving the pre-arrival anxiety window, mid-stay issues, and post-checkout dispute period entirely unaddressed, the precise moments where guest perception, review scores, and repeat bookings are actually won or lost. What makes this gap especially costly for growing operations is that VRBO does not natively support fully automated custom message templates the way Airbnb does. Hosts managing even a handful of listings find themselves writing the same check-in instructions, the same mid-stay check-ins, and the same review requests by hand, every single stay. That manual load compounds fast across multiple properties and markets, eroding both consistency and brand voice at exactly the moments guests are forming their impressions. Conduit's Workflows feature closes the gap: after a trigger event occurs in a conversation or guest lifecycle, a booking confirmation, a check-in, a detected keyword, Workflows fire the right message automatically, without a human in every thread. VRBO Automated Message Sequence - Quick-Reference Checklist # Message Type Timing Must-Include Elements Native VRBO Can Handle? 1 Booking Confirmation Within minutes of reservation Property address, direct contact, next-step preview ❌ No scheduled trigger 2 Pre-Arrival Welcome 72 hours before check-in (required) Arrival time, parking/access logistics, noise policies ✅ 7-day send only 3 Day-of Check-In Morning of arrival Door code, Wi-Fi password, one contact number ❌ No same-day trigger 4 Mid-Stay Check-In Midpoint of stay Open-ended check-in question, issue escalation path ❌ No mid-stay trigger 5 Checkout Reminder Evening before or morning of departure Checkout time, return-key instructions, tone of ease ❌ No checkout trigger 6 Post-Stay Review Request Promptly after checkout Personalized thank-you, direct review link ❌ No post-checkout trigger 72 hours VRBO's mandatory pre-arrival compliance window 1. Booking Confirmation Message - Set Expectations Before Excitement Fades The booking confirmation is the first VRBO automated message every host should deploy. Sent immediately after a reservation is accepted, it reassures guests their booking is secure, introduces the host's communication style, and plants early house-rule awareness. Hosts managing multiple properties benefit most since it eliminates repetitive manual replies. The tradeoff: overly long confirmations get skimmed, so brevity and warmth must be balanced carefully. 2. Pre-Arrival Check-In Instructions Message - Sent 72 Hours Before Stay VRBO now requires hosts to deliver entry instructions no later than 72 hours before check-in, making this automated message non-negotiable. It should include door codes, parking details, WiFi credentials, and a property address with map link. Hosts with smart locks benefit enormously since codes can be dynamically inserted. The limitation: if codes change per booking, your automation tool must support variable substitution or the message requires manual review before sending. 3. Day-of Check-In Welcome Message - The Digital Doorbell Greeting A warm, concise message sent on the morning of check-in day reminds guests of the check-in time window, confirms the property address, and invites them to reach out with questions. It functions as a digital handshake that reduces anxious guest calls and last-minute message floods. Hosts with self-check-in setups gain the most value here. The tradeoff is timing precision, sending too early feels irrelevant, too late feels rushed, so scheduling for 8--9 AM local time is the proven sweet spot. 4. Mid-Stay Check-In Message - The Silent Problem Catcher Sent 24--48 hours into the stay, a mid-stay VRBO automated message asks guests if everything is meeting expectations and whether they need anything. This single message is the most underused tool in a host's arsenal, it surfaces fixable issues before they become negative reviews. Hosts with longer average stays (5+ nights) see the greatest ROI. The tradeoff: for one-night stays this message arrives too late to be actionable, so trigger logic should exclude short bookings. 5. Checkout Reminder Message - Protect Your Turnover Window Sent the evening before or morning of departure, the checkout reminder outlines exactly what guests should do before leaving, stripping beds, starting the dishwasher, locking doors, and returning keys. It protects the host's cleaning window and reduces late checkouts that cascade into same-day turnover failures. Hosts with back-to-back bookings depend on this message most. The limitation: guests who feel micromanaged by overly detailed checklists may leave lukewarm reviews, so tone must stay friendly, not transactional. 6. Post-Stay Review Request Message - The Revenue-Compounding Closer Sent within 2--4 hours of checkout, a post-stay VRBO automated message thanks guests for their visit and gently encourages them to leave a review while the experience is still fresh. Reviews are the primary driver of VRBO search ranking and booking conversion, making this the highest-leverage message in the entire sequence. Hosts scaling beyond three properties see compounding returns as review velocity accelerates. The tradeoff: VRBO's communication policy restricts solicitation language, so the message must invite feedback naturally rather than explicitly demanding a five-star rating. The Real Limitations of VRBO's Native Automation (and When They Start to Hurt) VRBO's built-in messaging tools look functional until you try to scale with them. What most property managers discover too late is that the system's core constraints, static templates that require manual sends, broken links, and no conditional logic, don't just create friction; they quietly convert every edge case into a staff task. Understanding exactly where those limits sit is the first step to building a communication workflow that doesn't depend on someone remembering to log in. VRBO Templates Are Static by Design Most vacation rental property managers and operations leads think that once they set up VRBO's built-in automated messages, their guest communication is on autopilot and they can scale without adding staff time to messaging. In practice, there is a harder structural problem than most hosts realize going in: VRBO's so-called automated messages are not time-based automation at all. They are templates that require a host to manually log in, select, and send every single time. A guest who books a 14-night stay gets the same pre-arrival message as someone checking in for two nights, if the host remembers to send it. A guest who hasn't confirmed receipt of their access code gets no follow-up. The system has no awareness of those distinctions because it was never built to have any. The dysfunction compounds at the content level. Links sent through VRBO's native messaging system cannot be opened by guests, which means any automated message that includes a Google Doc, Google Maps link, or digital guidebook is effectively broken on arrival. Property managers who have invested time building out digital welcome packets or SOP-driven check-in guides discover this only after guests report they can't access the information. The message sends; the utility does not. This isn't a missing feature waiting on a product update. It's a design constraint of single-platform template systems. When a template can't read context and can't deliver clickable content reliably, every exception becomes a manual task. No Conditional Triggers "VRBO's so-called 'automated messages' are actually just templates that hosts must manually log in to select and send, there is no true time-based automation." There is no logic layer. There is no "if the guest hasn't responded to the check-in instructions within 12 hours, send a follow-up" path. There is no way to suppress a mid-stay check-in for a repeat guest who's stayed four times and clearly knows the property. The system fires on a schedule only when a human manually fires it, not on signal. That rigidity matters most precisely where automation creates the most leverage: recurring, predictable guest touchpoints that currently require manual staff action. Booking confirmation, day-of check-in support, mid-stay welfare checks, checkout reminders, and post-stay review requests are exactly the kind of structured, repeatable triggers that an event-driven system handles without staff involvement. VRBO's native toolset does not offer that logic layer. Without it, those touchpoints default back to a staff member making a judgment call on each booking, the opposite of scale. Platform Dependency as a Scaling Tax Industry research on multi-platform listing strategy consistently identifies distribution across multiple OTAs as a best practice for revenue stability and occupancy optimization. The problem is that every OTA runs its own native toolset, and automation configured on VRBO carries over to nothing. A manager running properties across VRBO, Airbnb, and a direct booking site is maintaining multiple separate template libraries, libraries that can never stay in sync, and that each require the same manual-send workflow. This is the scaling tax that single-platform automation imposes. The administrative load compounds with every new listing and every new channel. The impact is sharpest for operations teams managing guest communications across multiple platforms simultaneously, the exact scenario where a unified, cross-platform inbox and AI-driven workflow layer creates the most meaningful relief. When all guest conversations are visible and manageable in one place, and when the underlying automation can fire after a trigger event, a booking confirmed, a check-in completed, a specific keyword detected, the per-booking staff burden stops growing linearly with portfolio size. The Coverage Gap Across the Full Guest Journey The full guest journey includes pre-booking inquiries, booking confirmation, pre-arrival logistics, check-in support, mid-stay check-ins, issue escalation, checkout reminders, and post-stay review requests. VRBO's native system does not reliably handle any of these automatically , because without true time-based automation, each touchpoint depends on a staff member logging in and manually selecting the right template at the right moment. Booking confirmation, day-of check-in, mid-stay, checkout, and post-stay review requests are either entirely unscheduled or dependent on manual staff action. For businesses that already have existing documentation, SOPs, FAQs, property manuals, the gap between what those documents contain and what guests actually receive automatically is almost entirely a tooling problem, not a content problem. The information exists. The system to deliver it on the right trigger, to the right guest, across every platform, does not exist inside VRBO's native feature set. Third-Party Tools That Extend VRBO Automated Messages Beyond the Platform Third-party property management software is required for complete multi-channel automation on VRBO. No single native tool coordinates logic, timing, and guest data across multiple OTAs simultaneously. The tools below solve that architectural gap, each from a different angle. The real question is architectural, not cosmetic, but before evaluating any third-party tool, it is worth naming what that architecture is actually correcting for. Third-party tools don't merely supplement VRBO's native automation; they expose that native automation is not automation in any operationally meaningful sense. VRBO templates require per-platform manual duplication, cannot coordinate cross-channel logic, and carry documented glitch exposure even in tools designed to exceed them. For any operator managing multi-channel listings, the administrative overhead of maintaining platform-native systems grows proportionally with portfolio scale rather than compressing it, the exact inverse of the efficiency gain automation is supposed to deliver. Does the tool give you cross-channel consistency , event-driven logic, and dynamic guest data, all at once, across every OTA you list on? Tools that answer yes to all three move the needle. Tools that answer yes to only one or two shift the manual work around without eliminating it. A property manager running listings on VRBO, Airbnb, and a direct booking site has a coordination problem, not a template problem. Third-party tools collapse that overhead into a single logic layer. 1. Conduit.ai - Best AI-Powered VRBO Automated Messages Platform Conduit.ai sits above the PMS layer rather than replacing it. Its AI for hospitality platform catches the unscripted edge cases that template-based tools miss, using conversation-event triggers and live guest data to run follow-up actions autonomously. It is most beneficial when your business has recurring, predictable guest touchpoints that currently require manual staff action , check-in reminders, mid-stay check-ins, post-stay review requests, and you need those touchpoints handled consistently across every channel without a person moderating each one. The honest tradeoff: medium implementation complexity means it rewards operators with documented workflows, not those still building from scratch. 2. Hospitable - Best for Reliable Cross-Platform Message Delivery Hospitable delivers event-triggered, multi-step message sequences across VRBO, Airbnb, and direct bookings from a single dashboard, using dynamic data fields to personalize at each stage of the guest journey. Based on host community feedback, delivery reliability is meaningfully stronger than native VRBO tools, though not perfectly guaranteed. Hospitable is the best pick for solo hosts or small portfolios moving off native templates for the first time. 3. Hostaway - Best for Full VRBO Automation Beyond Just Messaging Hostaway combines channel management, messaging automation, and operations tooling in one platform. For property managers running large, multi-channel portfolios who need more than a messaging layer, Hostaway is the most comprehensive single-platform option evaluated here, though no independent benchmark data was identified during research, and operators should request a live demo against their specific channel mix before committing. It pays off at scale; it overwhelms a two-property host. If your portfolio is under ten units, the complexity-to-value ratio works against you. 4. OwnerRez - Best for Trigger-Based Scheduled VRBO Message Sequences OwnerRez offers trigger-based scheduled messaging that integrates directly with VRBO and other booking channels, giving hosts the ability to fire messages based on reservation events without relying on VRBO's native template library. It is best suited to hosts who want granular control over message timing and content and who already have a direct booking site they want to coordinate with. The tradeoff is a steeper configuration curve than simpler tools like Hospitable; operators who want quick setup over flexibility will find the learning investment higher than expected. 5. Uplisting - Best for Multi-Channel Hosts Centralizing VRBO Guest Messaging Uplisting centralizes VRBO automated messages alongside Airbnb and Booking.com communications in a single dashboard, letting hosts build one message template library that deploys across all channels simultaneously. It's the ideal fit for growing hosts who list on three or more platforms and can't afford to manage separate messaging workflows. The key limitation is that VRBO-specific message customization options are less granular than platform-dedicated tools. That gap between partial automation and a system that actually handles the full range of guest communication, across channels, contexts, and situations no template anticipated, is not a configuration problem. This section breaks down what creates the 40% ceiling, and what the infrastructure behind genuine automation actually requires. The 40% Ceiling and Why It Hits Fast Operators who have built out their VRBO template library often describe the same quiet frustration: the templates are live, the triggers are set, and the inbox is still full every morning. That frustration is not a setup error; it is a structural signal that the architecture underneath was never designed to handle what a real portfolio throws at it. VRBO's built-in automated message templates get operators to approximately 40% automation, after which they hit a ceiling when cross-channel consistency, dynamic guest data, and context-adaptive logic are required. The remaining 60%, late-night parking questions, mid-stay maintenance requests, cross-channel follow-ups from guests who booked on one platform and messaged on another, lands in someone's inbox because templates are static scripts. They fire on a schedule. They cannot read context, pull live booking data, or respond to a conversation event that was never anticipated when the template was written. Operators managing mid-sized portfolios feel this most acutely. Below a certain threshold, manual follow-up is annoying but survivable. Above it, the gap between 40% and genuine automation becomes a staffing problem no additional template can fix. What the Jump to 96% Actually Requires Erwan Le Roy's Cash Flow Street operation manages 35 properties and achieves a 96% automation rate, not because his VRBO templates are exceptionally well-written, but because he replaced the template trigger layer entirely. The workflow engine running his guest communication fires on live conversation events and dynamic guest data, not on a platform-specific schedule. That distinction is the whole game. Haven Vacation Rentals followed the same architectural path at larger scale. Starting at 40% automation, Haven reached 90% automation across 270 properties without proportionally growing its support headcount. The shift was not incremental template improvement; it was a categorical infrastructure change: moving from platform-scheduled messages to a workflow layer operating across SMS, WhatsApp, email, and internal team channels simultaneously, triggered by what is actually happening in the guest conversation. The Staffing Math Behind the Architecture Shift Easy BnB's story puts a number on what that shift is worth operationally. According to a Conduit customer case study, Conduit's AI-native coordination layer allowed Easy BnB to replace 14 virtual assistants. Darren, Easy BnB's founder, consolidated his VA layer across 75 units, generating substantial monthly savings while continuing to add properties without proportionally growing headcount. The honest trade-off: this transition requires upfront investment in workflow configuration and knowledge-base buildout. It is not plug-and-play, and operators with fewer than 10 properties may find the setup effort disproportionate to the immediate return. Most teams handle the gap between that threshold and full automation by adding people, another VA shift, a part-time coordinator, an overnight inbox manager. The hidden cost is not the salary line; it is that each person added manages per-channel rules manually, so reliability scales with human consistency rather than workflow logic. AI for hospitality platforms like Conduit close that gap by triggering on conversation events across every channel simultaneously, so the workflow engine decides what happens next rather than a person moderating a queue at midnight. Operators are running this infrastructure at scale today, and the entry point is more accessible than most property managers expect. The next section shows exactly what getting started looks like. VRBO's native system covers roughly 40% of the guest journey, leaving booking confirmation, mid-stay check-ins, and post-stay review requests either unscheduled or dependent on a staff member remembering to act. Start with our AI for hospitality . The structural ceiling matters here. VRBO's triggers fire only on booking-event schedules, which means the highest-stakes moments (pre-arrival anxiety, mid-stay issue windows, the two-hour post-checkout review window) are left entirely unaddressed by the platform. At the same time, the administrative overhead of maintaining platform-native templates grows with every new listing and every new channel, compounding in the exact direction automation is supposed to reverse. Together, those two facts point to the same conclusion: closing the gap between 40% and 90-plus percent automation requires replacing the trigger logic layer, not adding more templates to it. Start with conduit.ai to see how event-driven workflows handle the guest touchpoints VRBO's scheduling logic was never built to reach. From there, your existing SOPs and property documentation become the knowledge base the workflow engine draws from, so the messages guests receive are consistent, on-brand, and fired on the right signal, without a person moderating each thread. Frequently Asked Questions Does VRBO actually send automated messages on my behalf, or do I have to send them manually? VRBO sends only one genuinely scheduled message on your behalf: a welcome guide delivered 7 days before check-in. Everything else, including saved message templates, must still be manually selected and sent by a host or team member, because there is no trigger logic attached to them. I saved my VRBO message template, why didn't it send? Saving a template and activating a template are two separate actions in VRBO's system. A saved template sits in your library but will not fire until you explicitly enable it. The other most common causes of a silent failure are that the last-minute booking toggle is turned off, or the trigger window is set tighter than the booking lead time allows. What is the 'Always send for last-minute bookings and short stays' toggle and why does it matter? When a booking arrives close to check-in, a scheduled trigger can fall inside the lead time window and simply not fire, meaning your guest receives nothing. VRBO's toggle labeled 'Always send for last-minute bookings and short stays' is designed to prevent this, and for markets where a large share of bookings arrive close to check-in, it functions as a default requirement rather than an edge-case setting. Can an AI automatically answer guest questions on VRBO without me being in every thread? VRBO's native Inbox has no logic layer that reads a booking, evaluates context, and sends a message without manual intervention. conduit.ai's AI Agents close this gap by sitting above platform templates, once your SOPs and manuals are connected, the agent fires replies continuously before, during, and after a stay without manual intervention on each send. Which messages should I prioritize if I can only automate a few touchpoints right now? The post identifies the booking confirmation and the post-stay review request as the highest-stakes moments: the confirmation eliminates buyer's remorse within minutes of a reservation, and the review request must go out within roughly two hours of checkout while the stay is still vivid, review conversion drops sharply after that window closes. Both are moments VRBO's native toolset cannot cover with a scheduled trigger, making them the first gaps worth closing.

title: GE HealthCare expands breast imaging portfolio with Invenia ABUS Prime and launch of ABUS StreamVue
summary: GE HealthCare today announced the launch of Invenia™ ABUS (Automated Breast Ultrasound) Prime and ABUS StreamVue™, a redesigned enterprise viewer that recently received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) clearance and CE Marking, expanding its breast imaging portfolio with solutions designed for supplemental screening for women with dense breasts and provide more flexible enterprise-wide exam review.
body_text: Following the introduction of Invenia™ ABUS Prime at the Society of Breast Imaging Annual Symposium, the installation at BeSound in Los Angeles marks one of the first in the U.S., expanding access to supplemental screening for women with dense breasts ABUS StreamVue™* is a zero-footprint, browser-based reading solution designed to enable remote exam review from virtually anywhere across enterprise imaging networks and high-volume breast centers CHICAGO – August 3, 2026 — GE HealthCare today announced the launch of Invenia™ ABUS (Automated Breast Ultrasound) Prime and ABUS StreamVue™, a redesigned enterprise viewer that recently received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) clearance and CE Marking, expanding its breast imaging portfolio with solutions designed to support supplemental screening for women with dense breasts and provide more flexible enterprise-wide exam review. Together, these new solutions aim to help breast imaging programs standardize 3D ultrasound acquisition, support remote reading, and simplify deployment across multi-site networks. Studies conducted in the U.S. and Europe show 40% of women have dense breasts [1] , these women have a 4 to 6 times higher risk of developing breast cancer. [2] Dense breasts can make cancers harder to detect on mammography, and may delay diagnosis. [3] , [4] , [5] Research has shown that mammography may miss one-third of cancers in dense breasts, underscoring the need for supplemental screening options for these patients. [6] According to results from the Breast Screening: Risk Adaptive Imaging for Density study, ABUS demonstrated higher acceptance and a more positive patient experience compared to other contrast-enhanced techniques. [7] “Invenia ABUS Prime builds on our commitment to advancing supplemental breast screening for women with dense breasts,” said Karley Yoder, CEO, Ultrasound Solutions, Advanced Imaging Solutions, GE HealthCare. “As breast imaging networks look to scale across sites, Invenia ABUS Prime can help deliver streamlined workflows, reproducible imaging, with features designed to support both patient comfort and clinician efficiency.” When used alongside mammography, Invenia ABUS Prime supports earlier cancer detection. [8] Across growing breast imaging networks, the system helps support standardized exams, more efficient workflows and operational consistency, particularly in multi-site imaging environments. Invenia ABUS Prime features: cSound™ Imageformer with AI-enabled tools including Scan Quality Assessment and Auto Nipple Detection—powered by Verisound™ AI—developed to help deliver consistent, reproducible, high-quality scans and greater clinical confidence A Fast Scan tool that increases scan speed by up to 40%, along with a new-generation Reverse Curve™ transducer and selectable compression levels intended to enhance patient comfort and offer a more personalized patient experience [9] AI-supported reading powered by QVCAD™ is designed to streamline review. [10] AI Assistant powered by QVCAD has demonstrated a 33% reduction in reading time [11] and up to 93% sensitivity for lesion detection [12] ABUS StreamVue is a zero-footprint, browser-based reading solution built to standardize ABUS exam review with remote access and adaptable licensing intended to simplify installation, maintenance and growth for enterprise imaging environments. Candelis, Inc., a leading provider of innovative and cost-effective solutions to hospitals and imaging centers, is collaborating with GE HealthCare to deliver ABUS StreamVue technology in combination with Invenia ABUS. Together with Invenia ABUS Prime, this technology aims to facilitate faster reads, remote reading and easier comparisons across sites, while assisting IT teams in managing ultrasound systems more simply across the enterprise. “ABUS StreamVue extends the value of our ABUS platform with a flexible reading experience for enterprise imaging environments,” said Russ Behler, Global Product Director, LOGIQ Ultrasound, GE HealthCare. “This solution supports remote review, more standardized presentation, and simpler deployment across care settings.” Among the first U.S. installations of Invenia ABUS Prime is in Los Angeles at BeSound, which offers a modern breast imaging experience to expand access to supplemental breast cancer screening. BeSound is also planning a mobile screening unit to bring imaging services closer to patients. “At BeSound, our mission is to make supplemental breast screening more accessible and more convenient for the women who need it,” said Bailey Renger, Founder and CEO, BeSound. “With Invenia ABUS Prime, we hope to expand access to advanced breast imaging in a way that is patient-centered and meets women where they are.” Invenia ABUS Prime is U.S. FDA Premarket approved and CE Marked. Availability is subject to local regulatory approvals and may vary by country. ABUS StreamVue is U.S. FDA 510(k) cleared and CE Marked. [5] Tagliafico, Massimo Calabrese et al, Journal of Clinical Oncology 2016 34:16, 1882-188. [6] Mandelson et al. J Natl Cancer Inst 2000; 92:1081-1087.
